title: 7.2 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can go beyond today's lesson: solve one-step addition and subtraction equations using inverse operations in trickier cases, and explain WHY it works.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: Detective Chen tracked a suspect along the route shown in the case file. The route on Sunday was 6.6 kilometers longer than the route the suspect took on Saturday. The equation s + 6.6 = (Sunday's distance) shows the link. If Sunday's route was 13.2 kilometers, how many kilometers did the suspect travel on Saturday?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: The Evidence Locker
revealWordProblem.text: Detective Chen logs evidence bags into the agency vault. After she adds 18 new bags from today's case, the vault holds 64 bags in all. The equation b + 18 = 64 shows the situation, where b is the number of bags that were already in the vault. How many evidence bags were in the vault before today?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Subtract 18 from both sides: b = 64 − 18 = 46. There were 46 evidence bags in the vault before today. Check: 46 + 18 = 64 ✓

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do I solve an addition or subtraction equation?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Undo the operation with its inverse, and do it to both sides to keep the equation balanced — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Solve n + 23 = 58. The 23 is added to n.
The inverse of adding 23 is subtracting 23.
I subtract 23 from both sides: n + 23 − 23 = 58 − 23.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Use the balance scale to solve n + 23 = 58. What must you do to both sides to isolate n? As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.
hints: To isolate n, you need to remove the +23. What is the inverse of adding 23?
Subtract 23 from BOTH sides: n + 23 − 23 = 58 − 23 → n = 35.
explore.label: Solve the equation using the balance scale. Keep both sides equal!

discourse.prompt: Why do you have to subtract 23 from BOTH sides, not just one?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I subtract from both sides because an equation is like a ___ — to keep it balanced, any operation on one side must ___.

onLevel.stem: A shirt costs $d. After a $15 discount, it costs $38. What is d?
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: The $15 discount was taken OFF the original price d, and $38 is what's left after the discount.
Write the story first: d − 15 = 38. Then undo the subtraction — the original price should be MORE than $38, not less.
Add the $15 discount back onto the $38 sale price: d = 38 + 15. Which choice matches that total?

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Choose inverse
workedExample.work: The inverse of − 13 is + 13, so add 13 to both sides.

onLevel.correctWork: The inverse operation was correct, but the addition was done wrong: 28 + 13 = 41, not 31. So y = 41. Check: 41 − 13 = 28 ✓
hints: The plan (add 13 to both sides) is right. Recheck the arithmetic in the last step.
Add carefully: 28 + 13 = 41, so y = 41, not 31.

onLevel.title: Find the Equation Error
onLevel.correctWork: Inverse of subtraction is ADDITION. Add 18 to both sides: x = 45 + 18 = 63.
hints: Step 2 says the inverse of subtraction is subtraction. Is that right?
To undo −18, you need +18, not another −18. Addition undoes subtraction.

onLevel.prompt: A detective solved x + 25 = 60 and got x = 35. Another detective solved y − 25 = 60 and got y = 35. Are both correct? Explain using inverse operations and check each answer.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: For x + 25 = 60, the inverse operation is ___, so x = ___. Check: ___. For y − 25 = 60, the inverse operation is ___, so y = ___. Check: ___. Therefore, ___.
onLevel.hint: Use a strategy or example from the lesson to help you explain your answer.
hints: The two equations use OPPOSITE operations (+25 and −25), so the same inverse step cannot work for both.
Solve each with its own inverse: subtract 25 for x + 25 = 60, but add 25 for y − 25 = 60. Then substitute each result back into its equation.
Start with x + 25 = 60: subtract 25 from both sides and compare with the detective's 35. Then add 25 for the y equation and see whether 35 survives that check.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — Crack the Detective's Mistake
extending.correctWork: To undo + 8 you SUBTRACT 8 from both sides, not add: x + 8 − 8 = 21 − 8, so x = 13. Check: 13 + 8 = 21 ✓
hints: Step 3 adds 8 to both sides. Does adding 8 again remove the + 8?
The inverse of adding 8 is subtracting 8. Subtract 8 from both sides to isolate x.

extending.explanation: Subtract 9 from both sides: x = 15 − 9 = 6. Check: 6 + 9 = 15 ✓
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: x has 9 added to it. To get x alone, you need to UNDO that addition.
Use the inverse operation: subtraction undoes addition. Whatever you do, do it to BOTH sides to keep the balance.
Subtract 9 from both sides: x = 15 − 9. Then check by adding 9 back to your result — do you land on 15?

extending.explanation: Add 7 to both sides: y = 20 + 7 = 27. Check: 27 − 7 = 20 ✓
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: Look at what's happening to y: 7 is being SUBTRACTED. Which operation undoes subtraction?
Add the same amount to both sides so the equation stays balanced and y ends up alone.
Add 7 to both sides: y = 20 + 7. Check your result: does it minus 7 give back 20?

extending.explanation: Subtract 15 from both sides: n = 42 − 15 = 27. Check: 27 + 15 = 42 ✓
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: n is being increased by 15. To find n alone, you must undo that addition.
Subtract 15 from both sides — the +15 and −15 cancel on the left, leaving just n.
Compute 42 − 15 carefully (42 − 10 = 32, then take away 5 more). Check by adding 15 back to your answer.

extending.explanation: Add 11 to both sides: m = 25 + 11 = 36. Check: 36 − 11 = 25 ✓
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: m has 11 taken away from it. Think about which operation puts that 11 back.
Addition undoes subtraction: add 11 to both sides to leave m by itself.
Compute 25 + 11 for m. Then check: your answer minus 11 should equal 25.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake is applying the same operation instead of the inverse — for example, solving x − 7 = 15 by subtracting 7 from both sides (getting the wrong x = 8) instead of adding 7 to both sides (the correct x = 22). Another common mistake is doing the inverse operation to only one side, like solving x + 6 = 14 by subtracting 6 from the left but forgetting the right side. Before you submit, name the operation shown in the equation, choose its inverse, apply it to BOTH sides, and check by substituting your answer back into the original equation.

connect.scenario: A hiker has walked some distance and still has 4.5 miles left on a 12-mile trail. The equation d + 4.5 = 12 represents her situation, where d is the distance already walked.
connect.promptQuestion: How far has the hiker walked? How did you use inverse operations?
connect.prompt: The hiker walked ___ miles because d + 4.5 = 12 means d = 12 − ___ = ___.

exitTicket.explanation: Subtract 2.8 from both sides: p = 9.1 − 2.8 = 6.3. Check: 6.3 + 2.8 = 9.1 ✓ (11.9 comes from adding instead of subtracting; 7.7 comes from subtracting each decimal place without regrouping — 9 − 2 = 7 and, without borrowing, 8 − 1 = 7; 3.25 comes from dividing 9.1 ÷ 2.8 instead of subtracting.)
choiceFeedback: You added 2.8 — undo it by subtracting from both sides.
Recheck your subtraction: 9.1 − 2.8 in the tenths place.
Subtract 2.8 from 9.1 — that's not the result.
hints: p has 2.8 added to it. To get p alone you must undo the addition — decimals follow the same rule as whole numbers.
Subtract 2.8 from both sides. Line up the decimal points and watch the tenths place for regrouping.
Set up 9.1 − 2.8: you can't take 8 tenths from 1 tenth, so borrow from the 9 first. Then check by adding 2.8 back to your result.

questions.stem: Which equation represents: 'Three times a number equals 21'?
questions.explanation: 'Three times' means multiply by 3, so the equation is 3n = 21.

questions.stem: Which equation represents: 'Seven less than a number is 18'?
questions.explanation: 'Seven less than a number' means start with the number and subtract 7: n − 7 = 18.

questions.stem: Which equation represents: 'A number plus 12 equals 30'?
questions.explanation: 'Plus' means addition, so the equation is n + 12 = 30.
